2027-07-02.title: Friday of the sixth week after Pentecost · First Friday
readings: The churches of Macedonia gave themselves first to the Lord: abundant joy and extreme poverty overflowing in generosity
“I have shown you many good works from the Father”: believe the works, that the Father is in me and I am in the Father
2027-07-02.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Sixth Sunday after Pentecost. Today is the First Friday of the month. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam.
2027-07-02.verse: so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.
theo: Today is the First Friday of the month. Every Friday recalls the Cross, and many Catholic parishes give the first Friday of each month to special prayer, the Holy Qurbono and devotion to the Heart of Jesus, the heart that loved us to the end. Today's Epistle shows what such a heart looks like in those who follow him. St Paul writes to Corinth about the churches of Macedonia, the communities of Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, the first that he founded on European soil. They were small, poor, and already suffering. And Paul says of them: “for during a severe ordeal of affliction, their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.” Joy and poverty side by side, and out of them a flood of giving. They “voluntarily gave according to their means, and even beyond their means.” Usually it is the collector who has to beg. Here the givers do the begging: they were “begging us earnestly for the privilege of sharing in this ministry to the saints.”

Something more precious than money is named in the next verse: “they gave themselves first to the Lord and, by the will of God, to us.” The gift of self comes first and the gift of money follows from it. A parish that has given itself to the Lord is never short of gifts; a parish that gives only money, without itself, soon finds that even the money is hard to find. Paul does not command. He appeals to their pride in what is best in them: “Now as you excel in everything, in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in utmost eagerness, and in our love for you, so we want you to excel also in this generous undertaking.” A few verses later he gives the reason that stands behind all Christian giving: “For you know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Jesus gave himself first. The First Friday keeps this before our eyes: the Heart that was pierced on a Friday gave everything.

The Gospel carries us to the Temple at Jerusalem, in winter, at the Feast of the Dedication (John 10:22). Jesus has said, “The Father and I are one,” and some of his hearers pick up stones. When John writes “the Jews” in such a scene he means those in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus on that occasion; we must remember that Jesus himself, his Mother, the Apostles and the first Christians were all Jews, and the Church teaches that what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597). Jesus answers with calm: “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these are you going to stone me?” The works are his credentials: the sick healed, the hungry fed, the sinner forgiven. Then he argues from their own Scripture: “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods’?” If the Scripture could call those to whom the word of God came “gods”, can anyone say that “the one whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world is blaspheming because I said, ‘I am God's Son’?” The Fathers of the Church, especially in the East, drew from this the great truth that the Son of God became human so that we might share in his own life: “the Son of God became man so that we might become God,” wrote St Athanasius (On the Incarnation 54, in substance; Catechism 460).

Jesus ends with an invitation: “If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me. But if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.” Believe the works. The same test is put to us. The Macedonians' joy in their poverty was such a work: a sign that Christ was alive in them. Few people in our days are argued into faith; many are drawn when they see a neighbour who gives more than he can afford and ask where that comes from. John says that they tried to arrest Jesus again “but he escaped from their hands.” His hour had not yet come. Later in the same discourse he says, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18), and on a Friday he did. Today we ask for a heart like his, and for works that point to him.
outline: Ask: if someone looked at my works and not at my words, what would they say about the Father?
The churches of Macedonia give beyond their means and beg to be allowed to give.
The gift of self comes before the gift of money; Christ became poor for our sake.
The Father's works in Jesus; the Son of God became human so that we might share his life.
“they gave themselves first to the Lord”
live: Before giving anything this week, spend five minutes offering yourself to the Lord in prayer, and let the gift that follows come from that offering.
Choose one gift this week that costs you something, and give it with joy to a person or a cause in need.
Do one good work today that no one will notice, so that the Father may be seen in it.
2027-07-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, though you were rich, for our sake you became poor, so that by your poverty we might become rich. On this First Friday we look to your pierced Heart, which gave everything. Teach us to give ourselves first to you, and then whatever we have for the sake of your saints and your poor. Give us the joy of the churches of Macedonia, who found in their poverty a wealth of generosity. Let our works be so full of your love that those who see them may believe that you are in the Father and the Father is in you. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono Christ gives himself first, his Body and his Blood, and we are invited to give ourselves with him: whatever we bring to the altar is joined to the one offering of the Cross, which began in the heart of the Son who gave everything.

quick: The churches of Macedonia, in great affliction and poverty, gave beyond their means and begged for the privilege of giving.
Above all they gave themselves first to the Lord; Christ became poor for our sake so that we might become rich.
Jesus answers the stones with his works: “If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me.”
2027-07-02.action: Do one hidden act of generosity today and offer it to the Heart of Jesus on this First Friday.
2027-07-02.question: Have I given myself to the Lord first, or only what I have?

family.explain: St Paul tells the people of Corinth about some very poor Christians in Macedonia. They did not have much, but they were so happy in Jesus that they gave to others more than they could really afford, and they begged Paul to let them help. And the best thing they gave was themselves: first they gave themselves to the Lord. Jesus did the same for us. He was rich as God, and he became poor for our sake, and on a Friday he gave everything on the Cross. That is why we remember his Heart on every First Friday.
family.intention: We pray for families who are poor, and that our family may be glad to give.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we can give away this week, with joy?”

illus: A mason who worked on building sites in the Gulf came home to a village near Thiruvalla for his mother's funeral. He lived in a single rented room with five other men, and everyone knew he sent most of his wages home. At the funeral lunch the parish priest mentioned quietly that the church needed a few thousand rupees to repair a leaking roof over the old people's pew before the monsoon was in full spate. The next morning the mason came to the sacristy with an envelope; he would not say how much it held. The priest told afterwards that the roof was mended that week, and that when he thanked the man, the mason said only: my mother gave everything she had for us, and I do not know how else to learn to do it. The priest said that he had not heard a better sermon on the churches of Macedonia.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, on this First Friday we thank you for your Heart that gave everything. Teach us to give ourselves first to you, and make our works a sign of the Father's love. Amen.
share: Their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity (2 Corinthians 8:2). Where have I met joy in poverty?
They gave themselves first to the Lord (2 Corinthians 8:5). What would it mean for me to give myself first, before my gifts?
Believe the works (John 10:38). Which works of mine might lead someone toward the Father?
pm.resp: Lord, give us a heart like yours.
interc: For the Church, that she may give herself first to the Lord and so be generous to the poor.
For the poor and for those who suffer affliction, that they may find help from the generous.
For all who give beyond their means for the sake of others, that God may repay them with joy.
For those who find it hard to believe, that they may see in our works the love of the Father.
For our families, that we may learn to give with a glad heart on this First Friday.
pm.close: Father, you have shown us your good works in your Son. Give us the joy of those who give themselves first to you, and let our lives lead others to believe. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today is the First Friday, and we look to the Heart of Jesus, the Heart that gave everything. St Paul tells the Corinthians about the churches of Macedonia. They were poor and in affliction, and yet their abundant joy and their extreme poverty overflowed in a wealth of generosity (2 Corinthians 8:2). They gave according to their means, and even beyond their means, and they begged for the privilege of giving (2 Corinthians 8:3–4).

What was best of all is that they gave themselves first to the Lord (2 Corinthians 8:5). That is where all true giving begins. And Paul reminds us why: Jesus Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He gave himself first.

In the Gospel Jesus is threatened with stones, and he answers calmly: I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of these are you going to stone me? (John 10:32). He asks that people believe the works, so that they may know and understand that the Father is in him and he is in the Father (John 10:38). We too are to be known by our works. Many who do not read the Scriptures read our lives.
So today let us offer ourselves to the Lord first, and then let us give, with joy, even beyond our means, something that costs us. It will be a work that points to the Father. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know that today is the First Friday? We remember that Jesus loves us so much that he gave everything for us, even his life on the Cross. St Paul tells about some people who were very poor, but so happy in Jesus that they shared what little they had. And best of all, they gave themselves to the Lord. Today, do one kind thing without telling anyone: give a toy, help at home, or say a prayer for someone who is sad. That is how we show the Heart of Jesus to others.
